title: Comprehensive Guide to Congenital Cranial Dysinnervation Disorders (CCDD) & Strabismus Surgery
summary: An exhaustive clinical resource covering Duane Syndrome, Möbius Syndrome, Brown Syndrome, and complex Alphabet patterns. It details advanced surgical management including strengthening, weakening, transposition, and adjustable suture techniques.

branches: Failure of LR innervation by hypoplastic 6th nerve nucleus
Anomalous LR innervation by 3rd nerve fibers
Often bilateral condition
Approximately 10% familial; associated with gene mutations
Up to 50% have systemic defects (Deafness, External ear abnormalities, Speech disorder, Skeletal abnormalities)

sections.title: DRS Clinical Features
content: Typical face turn: Confers Binocular Single Vision (BSV) and avoids amblyopia
Abduction: Complete or partial restriction
Adduction: Restricted (usually partial)
Globe Retraction on adduction: Result of co-contraction of medial and lateral recti
Narrowing of palpebral fissure on adduction
Up-shoot or Down-shoot in adduction: Tight LR muscle slipping over/under the globe
Convergence Deficiency: Affected eye remains fixed in primary position while unaffected eye converges

sections.title: Management of Duane Syndrome
content: Non-Surgical: Majority do not need intervention. Children maintain BSV via Compensatory Head Posture (CHP).
Surgical Indications: Loss of binocular function (failure to use CHP), psychosocially unacceptable head posture, neck discomfort, severe up-shoots/down-shoots, or severe globe retraction.
Amblyopia: Usually results from anisometropia rather than strabismus.
Procedures: Unilateral/bilateral medial or lateral rectus recession. Transposition of SR and IR (or SR only) to LR to improve abduction.
Contraindication: Lateral rectus of the involved side should NOT be resected (increases retraction).

branches: Rare, usually sporadic
Brainstem developmental abnormality
Congenital non-progressive bilateral 6th and 7th cranial nerve palsies
Expressionless face (bilateral facial palsy)
Horizontal gaze palsy (50%)
Possible 5th, 8th, 10th, 12th CN involvement
Limb anomalies and mild mental handicap

sections.title: CFEOM & Strabismus Fixus
sections.content: Congenital Fibrosis of the Extraocular Muscles (CFEOM) is a rare non-progressive, autosomal dominant disorder (most commonly CFEOM1 via KIF21A mutation) featuring bilateral ptosis and restrictive external ophthalmoplegia. Pathologically, the superior division of the oculomotor nerve is hypoplastic. Eyes are typically fixed 10° below horizontal with compensatory chin elevation. Strabismus Fixus involves eyes fixed by fibrous tightening of the medial recti (convergent) or lateral recti (divergent), in both congenital and acquired forms.

rows: Inability to elevate eye from abduction to adduction; tight IR or hypoplastic SR
Limited elevation in adduction; can be congenital or acquired
Congenital ptosis, horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, congenital 4th/7th palsy
Chin-up; Face-turn away from affected eye

sections.title: Brown Syndrome Management
content: Congenital: Usually no treatment if BSV/posture are maintained. Spontaneous improvement often by end of 1st decade.
Congenital Surgery: Recommended if significant hypotropia or deteriorating control. Procedure: Lengthening of superior oblique tendon.
Acquired Causes: Trauma to trochlea, inflammation (RA, pansinusitis, scleritis).
Acquired Treatment: Address specific etiology; steroids (oral or peritrochlear injection).

branches: Causes: IO overaction (4th palsy), SO underaction, SR underaction, Brown syndrome
Treatment (Oblique): IO weakening or SO strengthening
V-Eso Treatment: MR recession + downward transposition
V-Exo Treatment: LR recession + upward transposition
Causes: Primary SO overaction, IO underaction/palsy, IR underaction
Treatment (Oblique): SO posterior tenotomy (20Δ) or total tenotomy (50Δ)
A-Eso Treatment: MR recession + upward transposition
A-Exo Treatment: LR recession + downward transposition

content.explanation: Before surgical realignment, any significant refractive error and/or underlying amblyopia MUST be corrected.

sections.title: Strengthening Procedures
content: Resection: Muscle exposed, absorbable sutures inserted at measured distance, muscle excised anteriorly, reattached to original insertion.
Plication (Tucking): Fold muscle; less traumatic, preserves anterior ciliary vessels, reversible. Used for recti or lax SO.
Advancement: Moving previously recessed muscle closer to the limbus.

sections.title: Weakening Procedures
content: Rectus Recession: Suture outer quarters, disinsert, measure/mark sclera, resuture at measured distance (or hang-back).
Inferior Oblique Recession: Exposed via inferotemporal fornix, disinserted, sutured 3mm posterior/temporal to temporal IR insertion edge.
Disinsertion (Myectomy): Detaching without reattachment (commonly for overacting IO).
Posterior Fixation (Faden): Suture muscle belly to sclera (or pulley) 12mm posteriorly to decrease pull in field of action without affecting primary position.

sections.title: Transposition & Specialized Surgery
sections.content: Transposition relocates muscles to substitute for absent/deficient action, most commonly for severe LR weakness in 6th nerve palsy, Duane syndrome, alphabet patterns, and MED. Techniques involve recti and oblique muscles. Vector adjustment procedures primarily aim to alter the direction of muscle action.

sections.title: Adjustable Suture Techniques
content: Step 1: Indications - Precise outcome needed (Restrictive strabismus, trauma, previous surgery, Duane/Möbius/Myasthenia, complex deviations).
Step 2: Operative - Muscle sutures passed through stump; Noose knot tied; Ends tied in a loop; Conjunctiva left open.
Step 3: Adjustment (Post-Op) - Perform under topical anesthesia when patient is awake.
Step 4: More Recession - Pull noose knot anteriorly to provide slack; patient looks towards field of action.
Step 5: Less Recession - Pull muscle suture anteriorly and tighten knot against stump.
Step 6: Completion - Once aligned, secure main knot, remove loop, close conjunctiva.

sections.title: Complications of Strabismus Surgery
content: Operative: Lost or 'slipped' muscle (especially Medial Rectus).
Operative: Globe perforation by misplaced suture (risk high in thin-sclera high myopia).
Operative: Opening posterior Tenon capsule leading to fat/muscle fibrosis (risk in IO surgery).
Postoperative: Over-correction and Under-correction (may require reoperation).
Postoperative: Anterior segment ischaemia (Avoid removing >2 rectus muscles at once; more common in elderly).
Postoperative: Stretched scar (can occur years later, causing malalignment).
